literal: Yuan clearly understood institutions, knew many old precedents, and with Masters of Writing Cui Xuanbo jointly fixed court ritual, laws and orders, music, and military and state records, edicts and policies — most of it was Yuan's work.
idiomatic: Yuan had a clear grasp of institutions and old precedent; with Cui Xuanbo of the Masters of Writing he shaped court ritual, statutes, music, and the military and state archives, edicts and policies — most of it was Yuan's hand.

literal: On the campaign against Pingyang he was rewarded with the enfeoffment Marquis of Hankang; it was changed to Marquis of Xiabo and he was made General of the Central Rampart.
idiomatic: On the Pingyang campaign he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Hankang, then made Marquis of Xiabo and general of the central rampart.

literal: The Founding Emperor ordered Yuan to compile the national record; Yuan produced more than ten scrolls, only year-by-year daily affairs and conduct, with no formal pattern yet.
idiomatic: The Founding Emperor charged Yuan to compile the national record; he drafted more than ten scrolls of year-by-year court affairs only, without a settled form.

literal: Yuan was scrupulous in court business and never went against the throne's intent.
idiomatic: Yuan was exacting in court affairs and never crossed the sovereign's will.

literal: His younger cousin by the father's line, Hui, was a Masters of Writing gentleman — fierce and fond of adventure, thick friends with Marquis of Dingling He Ba.
idiomatic: His father's younger cousin's son Hui was a gentleman in the Masters of Writing — violent, restless, and close to Marquis of Dingling He Ba.

literal: When Ba was executed for crime, his sons and younger brothers fled to Chang'an; someone reported that Hui would send them out.
idiomatic: When Ba was put to death for his crimes, his kin fled to Chang'an; someone said Hui meant to smuggle them out.

literal: Thereupon the Founding Emperor suspected Yuan knew of it and ordered Yuan to die; afterward he regretted it.
idiomatic: The Founding Emperor then suspected Yuan had known and had Yuan put to death — and afterward regretted it.

literal: Men of the time all pitied him.
idiomatic: All who heard of it mourned him.

literal: His son Ying inherited the enfeoffment.
idiomatic: His son Ying succeeded to the title.

literal: He was a student of the Imperial Academy and was gradually promoted to Attendant in the Secretariat.
idiomatic: He studied at the Imperial Academy and rose step by step to secretariat attendant.

literal: Emperor Shizu ordered Grand Minister of Ceremonials Cui Hao to gather literary men to compile the dynastic history; Ying, with Hao's younger brother Lan and others, all took part in the writing.
idiomatic: Emperor Shizu ordered Grand Minister of Ceremonials Cui Hao to gather scholars to compile the dynastic history; Ying joined Hao's brother Lan and others on the work.

literal: When the imperial carriage visited the desert south, the Gaoche chieftain Mofu Kugan led tens of thousands of horsemen driving more than a million deer to the traveling palace.
idiomatic: When the court visited the southern desert, the Gaoche chief Mofu Kugan brought tens of thousands of riders driving more than a million deer to the encampment.

literal: An edict made Ying compose a text and inscribe it in the desert south to record the achievement.
idiomatic: Ying was ordered to write and set up an inscription in the southern desert to commemorate the feat.

literal: He was also made Acting Regular Attendant and sent on mission to Liu Yilong.
idiomatic: He was also made acting regular attendant and sent as envoy to Liu Yilong.

literal: He was advanced to marquis and made Dragon-Charging General.
idiomatic: He was raised to marquis and made dragon-charging general.

literal: In Yanhe year 3 he followed the campaign against the Hu bandit Bai Long.
idiomatic: In Yanhe year 3 he joined the campaign against the Hu rebel Bai Long.

literal: On the return he died on the road.
idiomatic: He died on the march home.

literal: Posthumous title Wengong.
idiomatic: His posthumous name was Wengong.

literal: His son Yi inherited.
idiomatic: His son Yi succeeded.

literal: He reached the posts Inspector of Jingzhou and Acting Pacifying-South General.
idiomatic: He rose to Jingzhou inspector and acting pacifying-south general.

literal: He was granted the enfeoffment Duke of Nanyang.
idiomatic: He was enfeoffed as Duke of Nanyang.

literal: He died in the Heping era.
idiomatic: He died in the Heping era — so the record runs.

literal: His eldest son Liangnu inherited.
idiomatic: His eldest son Liangnu succeeded.

literal: Liangnu's younger brother attended Emperor Gaozu and was granted the name Shu.
idiomatic: Liangnu's younger brother attended Emperor Gaozu and was given the name Shu.

literal: He passed through civil offices and was praised for integrity and caution.
idiomatic: He served in civil posts and was praised for upright care.

literal: He was moved to Grand Master of the Palace and Acting Vice Director of the Court of Justice.
idiomatic: He was promoted to grand master of the palace and acting vice director of the court of justice.

literal: He went out as General Who Establishes Loyalty and Inspector of Qi Province.
idiomatic: He went out as general who establishes loyalty and Qi inspector.

literal: When the hundred offices were first reorganized, the chief aides of the great offices were newly weighted.
idiomatic: At the first reshaping of the hundred offices, chief aides to the great ministries were given new weight.

literal: At that time the Grand Tutor Yuan Pi went out as Inspector of Bing Province; Shu was made Chief Clerk to the Grand Tutor, concurrently Taiyuan Administrator.
idiomatic: When Grand Tutor Yuan Pi went out as Bing inspector, Shu was made his chief clerk and concurrently Taiyuan administrator.

literal: Soon he was summoned as Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works and died in office.
idiomatic: Soon he was recalled as chief clerk to the minister of works and died in his post.

literal: An edict granted one hundred thousand cash and fifty bolts of cloth; posthumous name Zhen.
idiomatic: The throne granted one hundred thousand cash and fifty bolts of cloth; his posthumous name was Zhen.

literal: His eldest son Zuan was a court attendant and rose through posts to Grand Master of the Palace.
idiomatic: His eldest son Zuan was a court attendant and rose to grand master of the palace.

literal: Zuan's younger brother Xian was court attendant, Sacrificer in the Western Pavilion of the Minister of Works, Outer Regular Attendant, and Magistrate of Heyin.
idiomatic: Zuan's younger brother Xian was court attendant, sacrifier in the minister of works' western pavilion, outer regular attendant, and Heyin magistrate.

literal: Soon he was moved to General Who Pacifies the Distance and Remonstrance and Policy Grand Master.
idiomatic: Soon he was made general who pacifies the distance and remonstrance and policy grand master.

literal: At the end of Emperor Suzong's reign he was made Champion General and Inspector of Ying Province.
idiomatic: Late in Emperor Suzong's reign he was made champion general and Ying inspector.

literal: At the opening of the Jianyi era, hearing that Erzhu Rong had entered Luoyang and court gentlemen were being killed, he fled to Xiao Yan.
idiomatic: At the opening of Jianyi, when he heard Erzhu Rong had entered Luoyang and courtiers were being killed, he fled to Xiao Yan.

literal: Yi's younger brother Zongqing, from a student of the Secretariat, entered service as Central Court Attendant.
idiomatic: Yi's younger brother Zongqing, starting as a secretariat student, entered service as central court attendant.

literal: He was gradually promoted to Masters of Writing, with Acting Regular Attendant added, and granted the enfeoffment Marquis of Ding'an.
idiomatic: He rose step by step to the Masters of Writing, was given acting regular attendant, and enfeoffed as Marquis of Ding'an.

literal: He was transferred to Director of the Southern Bureau.
idiomatic: He was shifted to director of the southern bureau.

literal: Zongqing spent many years in the Southern Bureau and submitted many memorials; provinces and garrisons feared him, and he was called competent.
idiomatic: Zongqing spent years in the southern bureau and filed many memorials; provinces and garrisons feared him and called him fit for the post.

literal: He was advanced to Duke of Nanyang, made Pacifying-South General and Inspector of Jing Province, then enfeoffed as Duke of Zhao Commandery.
idiomatic: He was raised to Duke of Nanyang, made pacifying-south general and Jing inspector, then enfeoffed as Duke of Zhao Commandery.

literal: In the province Zongqing was sued by the people; though inquiry and trial proved the facts, high and low were deeply at odds.
idiomatic: In his province the people brought suit against Zongqing; though investigation proved the charges, he and they were utterly estranged.

literal: He was transferred to Inspector of Xu Province, still holding the same general's title.
idiomatic: He was moved to Xu inspector while keeping the same army title.

literal: Before long, because his wife Han practiced witchcraft, he was executed.
idiomatic: Before long his wife Han was found guilty of witchcraft and he was put to death.

literal: Zongqing's son Boxin died with his father.
idiomatic: Zongqing's son Boxin died with him.

literal: Boxin's son Yan fled south and escaped.
idiomatic: Boxin's son Yan fled south and survived.

literal: Later he served as Masters of Writing gentleman, was made Administrator of Changshan, then Pacifying-South General, Grand Master of Splendid Virtue, Bearer of the Staff, Acting Left Deputy Director of the Masters of Writing and Jingzhou Mobile Headquarters, and again Pacifying-Army General.
idiomatic: Later he was a Masters of Writing gentleman, then Changshan administrator, then pacifying-south general, grand master of splendid virtue, bearer of the staff, acting left deputy director of the Masters of Writing and mobile headquarters for Yingzhou, and again pacifying-army general.

literal: He died; posthumously made Pacifying-South General and Inspector of Jing Province.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously made pacifying-south general and Jing inspector.

literal: Ying's younger brother Quan followed Emperor Shizu on campaigns and reached Dragon-Charging General, Inspector of Yu Province, and the enfeoffment Marquis of Xinye.
idiomatic: Ying's younger brother Quan followed Emperor Shizu in war and rose to dragon-charging general, Yu inspector, and Marquis of Xinye.

literal: On campaign against the Rouran he was executed for an offense.
idiomatic: On the Rouran campaign he was executed for a breach of law.

literal: His younger brother Hao died as Attendant in the Secretariat.
idiomatic: His younger brother Hao died while secretariat attendant.

literal: Hao's eldest son Lingzhen was a Secretariat student and [24] Secretariat Central Court Attendant.
idiomatic: Hao's eldest son Lingzhen was a secretariat student and [24] secretariat central court attendant.

literal: He died; posthumously made Outer Acting Regular Attendant.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously made outer acting regular attendant.

literal: His son Xian passed through Secretariat student and Attending Censor and was known for clarity and care.
idiomatic: His son Xian served as secretariat student and attending censor and was known for sharp judgment and care.

literal: He went out as Chief Clerk on the campaign staff of Prince of Wuchang, General Who Campaigns Against the Barbarians.
idiomatic: He went out as chief clerk on Prince of Wuchang's campaign staff as general who campaigns against the barbarians.

literal: Later when Li Yuanhu held Qi Province, Xian remained chief clerk and concurrently Administrator of Eastern Wei Commandery.
idiomatic: When Li Yuanhu later held Qi, Xian stayed as chief clerk and concurrently eastern Wei commandery administrator.

literal: In office ten years, through three inspectors, he was famed for pure diligence.
idiomatic: Ten years in office under three inspectors, he was famed for clean, tireless service.

literal: The people of Qi cherished his kindness and called him a true two-thousand-dan.
idiomatic: The people of Qi cherished him and called him a true two-thousand-dan magistrate.

literal: When he was replaced and returned, he received many parting gifts from the people — and was somewhat harmed by this.
idiomatic: On his recall he accepted heavy farewell gifts from the people, and his reputation suffered for it.

literal: Prince of Zhongshan Ying attacked Yiyang; Xian was army supervisor.
idiomatic: Prince of Zhongshan Ying attacked Yiyang; Xian served as army supervisor.

literal: When it ended he was made Remonstrance and Policy Grand Master and Acting Attendant at the Yellow Gate, assisting Attendant You Zhao as metropolitan envoy.
idiomatic: When the campaign ended he was made remonstrance and policy grand master and acting attendant at the yellow gate, assisting You Zhao as metropolitan envoy.

literal: Later he paid bribes to the Recording Masters of Writing, Prince of Beihai Xiang, and was moved to Vice Minister of the Grand Granary.
idiomatic: Later he bribed Recording Masters of Writing Prince of Beihai Xiang and was moved to vice minister of the grand granary.

literal: He conducted affairs of Jing Province, was moved to General Who Campaigns Against the Barbarians and Inspector of Ying Province, and garrisoned Yiyang.
idiomatic: He handled Jingzhou affairs, then was made general who campaigns against the barbarians and Ying inspector, garrisoning Yiyang.

literal: In the province he was sharp at levying taxes.
idiomatic: In his province he was fierce in levying taxes.

literal: He also paid bribes to Yu Zhong and was summoned as Attendant at the Yellow Gate.
idiomatic: He also bribed Yu Zhong and was recalled as attendant at the yellow gate.

literal: Soon he was made Rear General and Intendant of Henan, with the yellow gate post unchanged.
idiomatic: Soon he was made rear general and Henan intendant while keeping the yellow gate post.

literal: Before he took the appointment, Empress Dowager Ling held court; Yuan Zhao was made Intendant of Henan and Xian remained at the yellow gate, with Pacifying-South General added.
idiomatic: Before he could take up the post, Empress Dowager Ling held court; Yuan Zhao was made Henan intendant while Xian stayed at the yellow gate and was given pacifying-south general.

literal: For his merit as army supervisor at Yiyang, Xian was enfeoffed as Viscount of Anyang with an estate of three hundred households.
idiomatic: For his service as Yiyang army supervisor, Xian was enfeoffed as Viscount of Anyang, estate three hundred households.

literal: Xian curried favor with those close to the throne, and therefore received the enfeoffment.
idiomatic: Xian courted those about the throne, and so won the fief.

literal: At that time You, Ying, Cang, and Ji suffered great floods, repeated raids, and the people were hungry.
idiomatic: You, Ying, Cang, and Ji then suffered great floods, repeated raids, and famine among the people.

literal: An edict made Xian Acting Masters of Writing and Acting Regular Attendant, Bearer of the Staff sent to the provinces to relieve according to local need; he aided many.
idiomatic: Xian was made acting Masters of Writing and acting regular attendant, bearer of the staff sent through the provinces to relieve distress where needed, and helped many.

literal: At the opening of the Shengui era an abscess broke out and he died, age fifty-four.
idiomatic: At the opening of Shengui an abscess broke out and he died at fifty-four.

literal: An edict granted three hundred bolts of silk for funeral expenses and one suit of court dress; posthumously made Pacifying-East General and Inspector of Qing Province, posthumous name Gong.
idiomatic: The throne granted three hundred bolts of silk for the funeral and one court robe; posthumously he was made pacifying-east general and Qing inspector, posthumous name Gong.

literal: His eldest son Ji, styled Bosheng, had considerable aspiration.
idiomatic: His eldest son Ji, styled Bosheng, had real ambition.

literal: Secretariat gentleman.
idiomatic: He was a secretariat gentleman.

literal: Court discussion held that because Xian by origin did not merit a mountains-and-rivers reward, Ji was not allowed to inherit.
idiomatic: Court debate held that Xian had not truly earned a territorial fief, so Ji was not allowed to succeed.

literal: Ji sued and pleaded for a long time before he was at last permitted to receive the enfeoffment.
idiomatic: Ji pleaded at law for a long time before succession was finally granted.

literal: He was gradually moved to Front General, Grand Master of the Palace, and Chief Clerk of the Liang Province headquarters.
idiomatic: He rose step by step to front general, grand master of the palace, and chief clerk of the Liang headquarters.

literal: With Inspector Yuan Luo he alike fell into Xiao Yan's hands and died in the south.
idiomatic: He and Inspector Yuan Luo alike fell to Xiao Yan and died in the south.

literal: His son Xiaoxu, in the Yuanxiang era, brought Ji's coffin back to the realm.
idiomatic: His son Xiaoxu, in the Yuanxiang era, brought Ji's coffin home.

literal: In the Xinghe era he inherited the enfeoffment.
idiomatic: In the Xinghe era he succeeded to the title.

literal: When Qi received the mandate, by precedent the rank was reduced.
idiomatic: When Qi took the throne, the rank was reduced by rule.

literal: Lingzhen's younger brother Lingqi was General Who Establishes Loyalty and Inspector of Qi Province.
idiomatic: Lingzhen's younger brother Lingqi was general who establishes loyalty and Qi inspector.

literal: His title was advanced to Champion General and he was granted the enfeoffment Marquis of Changguo.
idiomatic: His title was raised to champion general and he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Changguo.

literal: His government was pure and simple; he had authority and kindness.
idiomatic: His rule was plain and clean, with both sternness and grace.

literal: His son Gongbo was Right Grand Master of Splendid Virtue.
idiomatic: His son Gongbo was right grand master of splendid virtue.

literal: The historiographer says: To steer the state and shepherd the people, none fails to combine civil and military.
idiomatic: The historiographer writes: To govern a state and tend its people, none can do without both civil and military craft.

literal: Yan Feng, with broad learning and many hearths, won Zhaocheng's courtesy; he harmonized neighbors and preserved the state — is this not the effect of worth?
idiomatic: Yan Feng's wide learning won Emperor Zhaocheng's courtesy; he soothed neighbors and kept the state whole — the work of a worthy man.

literal: Xu Qian's talent and method were both fine; in galloping through hard days he alone read the moment and urged advance — his cause matched a hidden tally.
idiomatic: Xu Qian united talent and method; in the hurrying days of crisis he alone saw the hour and urged advance — as if fate itself had marked him.

literal: Zhang Gun was known for talent and stratagem, early favored; when the age lacked lenient rule, that saying brought blame.
idiomatic: Zhang Gun was prized for talent and counsel and favored early; in an age without gentle government, his words drew reproach.

literal: Xuanbo's house was lofty through generations and still stood at the founding; he bore the weight of the pivot, kept to the straight path and finished the work — ritual from the clear temple: was it not fitting?
idiomatic: Xuanbo's clan was great for generations and still stood at the founding; he carried the state's pivot, held the straight course and finished the work — rites worthy of the ancestral temple: could it have been otherwise?

literal: Kuan and Mo alike could see the moment and act; when the Way was blocked they still gave their allegiance.
idiomatic: Cui Kuan and Cui Mo alike saw the hour and moved; when the Way was shut they still pledged their allegiance.

literal: Deng Yuan was upright and white in service, talented in wielding the brush; disaster was not his crime — how sad!
idiomatic: Deng Yuan was upright in office and skilled with the brush; his fall was not his crime — a bitter loss!

literal: Collation notes
idiomatic: Textual notes

literal: Gongda gave himself to Wei Wu. In various editions "da" is written as "yuan"; Cefu juan 765
idiomatic: "Gongda gave himself to Wei Wu": editions read da (達) as yuan (遠); Cefu juan 765

literal: 〈page 9095〉
idiomatic: folio 9095

literal: reads "da".
idiomatic: has "da".

literal: Commentary: Xun You's style was Gongda
idiomatic: Note: Xun You's style was Gongda

literal: 〈Records of the Three Kingdoms, juan 10〉
idiomatic: Records of the Three Kingdoms, juan 10

literal: , among Cao Cao's famed assistants none is heard of as "Gongyuan"; now emended according to Cefu.
idiomatic: ; among Cao Cao's famed counselors no "Gongyuan" is known — emended per Cefu.
